name: Patent Filings
blurb:
This section tracks cumulative AI-related patent counts for 108 companies, ranking them by total portfolio size and charting how the combined total moves over time. It answers who is building the largest patent positions in AI, not who is inventing the most cutting-edge techniques right now, since raw filing counts favor large, long-established portfolios over newer, more selective filers.

The total is checked daily but only changes in step jumps every five to seven days, so it is best read as a periodically refreshed patent-database snapshot rather than a live daily count of new filings. Filing databases also lag actual invention by months given publication delays, and patent volume says nothing about which filings cover techniques that matter commercially or turn out to be defensible.

As of September 5, 2026, the tracked total stands at 312,470 AI-related patents across the 108 companies, up from 310,516 three weeks earlier, a gain of about 1,954 patents, or roughly 650 per week. Samsung leads by a wide margin with 108,943 patents, more than the next three companies combined, IBM at 69,827, Apple at 31,794, and Huawei at 27,442. Microsoft follows at 24,682. Further down, chip and model companies file far less by volume. NVIDIA holds 3,489, Meta 2,684, and Palantir 1,668, reflecting narrower but more targeted AI patent strategies. The count also tracks granted patents rather than pending applications, so it understates real activity for companies whose recent filings are still in prosecution and have not yet issued.

reading.body:
Patent volume concentrates heavily in established tech companies, not the AI chipmakers and model builders leading compute scaling. Samsung, IBM, and Apple hold more than half of the 312,470 tracked patents across 108 companies, while NVIDIA, the dominant AI chip supplier, ranks tenth with only 3,489 patents.

This gap reflects different business models and patent strategies rather than innovation capacity. Hardware and software incumbents file broadly across decades of product lines and defensible prior art. Specialized AI companies file narrowly on core techniques, treating patents as one tool among many rather than the primary IP protection. A company filing 100,000 patents across consumer electronics, networking, and storage builds a defensive moat. A chipmaker filing 3,000 patents on GPU architecture and compute kernels may be innovating faster in AI specifically.

The count measures granted patents, not pending applications or actual invention dates. Filing databases lag actual work by months. This means the data shows completed legal protection, not current research intensity or the speed at which new techniques are being generated. For understanding where AI capabilities are being built right now, patent volume is a measure of historical defensive positioning, not forward momentum. It does not tell you which companies are winning the race to scale compute or who will control the buildings and power that constrain it next.
